flashcards.front: What is objective 1 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Explain the PAVE checklist including Pilot assessment (medical, currency, proficiency, fatigue, stress, knowledge - IMSAFE checklist), Aircraft assessment (documents, equipment, maintenance, condition), enVironment assessment (weather, airspace, terrain, airports), and External pressures (time, money, passengers, personal pressures)

flashcards.front: What is objective 2 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Assess pilot readiness including IMSAFE checklist (Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion), medical certificate validity, currency requirements (flight review, recent flight experience, night currency, instrument currency), proficiency level (comfortable with planned flight, adequate experience), and personal factors (well-rested, alert, manageable stress)

flashcards.front: What is objective 3 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Assess aircraft airworthiness including documents (airworthiness certificate, registration, operating limitations), required equipment (Part 91.205 VFR day/night equipment, all operational), maintenance (annual inspection within 12 months, 100-hour inspection if used for hire within 100 hours, AD compliance), and condition (safe condition, adequate fuel/oil, no damage, proper configuration)

flashcards.front: What is objective 4 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Assess environmental factors including weather (current conditions, forecasts, advisories - visibility, clouds, wind, thunderstorms, icing), airspace (controlled airspace requirements, restrictions, NOTAMs), terrain (obstacles, elevation, routes), and airports (runway conditions, services, NOTAMs)

flashcards.front: What is objective 5 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Identify external pressures including time pressure (schedule, deadlines, running late), financial pressure (cost of cancellation, fuel costs), passenger pressure (expectations, commitments, waiting passengers), and personal pressure (pride, ego, proving something, not wanting to cancel)

flashcards.front: What is objective 6 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Make go/no-go decisions including evaluating all PAVE factors systematically, determining if all factors are acceptable (GO) or any factor is questionable (NO-GO), identifying alternatives (delay, cancel, change route/aircraft/pilot), and prioritizing safety over external pressures

flashcards.front: What is objective 7 for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Teach preflight assessment to students effectively explaining PAVE checklist, pilot assessment, aircraft assessment, environment assessment, external pressures, and go/no-go decision-making with integrated scenarios

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: PAVE checklist provides systematic preflight assessment: P - Pilot (are you ready? IMSAFE checklist, medical, currency, proficiency, fatigue, stress, knowledge), A - Aircraft (is aircraft ready? documents, equipment, maintenance, condition), V - enVironment (is environment suitable? weather, airspace, terrain, airports), E - External pressures (are there pressures affecting decision? time, money, passengers, personal)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Pilot assessment using IMSAFE checklist: I - Illness (are you sick? feeling unwell? if ill, don't fly), M - Medication (are you taking medication? check side effects, if medication affects performance, don't fly), S - Stress (are you stressed? personal, work, emotional stress affects performance, if stress significant, evaluate carefully), A - Alcohol (8-hour bottle-to-throttle minimum, 24 hours recommended, if alcohol consumed, don't fly), F - Fatigue (are you tired? well-rested? adequate sleep? if tired, don't fly), E - Emotion (are you emotionally ready? personal issues? if emotional state questionable, evaluate carefully)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Pilot factors assessment: Medical (valid medical certificate, feeling well, no illness - private pilot third-class valid 60 months if under 40, 24 months if 40 or older), Currency (flight review within 24 months, recent experience recommended within 90 days, night currency 3 takeoffs/landings within 90 days, instrument currency 6 approaches within 6 months), Proficiency (comfortable with planned flight, adequate experience, familiar with aircraft/route/conditions), Fatigue (well-rested, alert, adequate sleep - 7-9 hours recommended), Stress (manageable stress, no significant personal/work/emotional stress), Knowledge (understand flight requirements, weather, procedures)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Aircraft assessment: Documents (airworthiness certificate present and valid, registration present and current, operating limitations POH/AFM present), Equipment (required equipment operational - Part 91.205 VFR day: airspeed, altimeter, compass, engine instruments, fuel gauges, ELT; VFR night: all day equipment plus position lights, anti-collision lights, landing light, electrical system), Maintenance (annual inspection within 12 months, 100-hour inspection if used for hire within 100 hours, all ADs complied with), Condition (aircraft in safe condition, no damage, proper configuration, adequate fuel/oil, no leaks, controls free and correct)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Environment assessment: Weather (current conditions METARs, forecasts TAFs, advisories AIRMETs/SIGMETs - visibility meets VFR minimums 3 statute miles, clouds meet VFR minimums 500 feet below/1,000 feet above/2,000 feet horizontal, wind within limits, avoid thunderstorms completely, avoid icing in winter), Airspace (controlled airspace Class B/C/D/E requirements, restrictions TFRs, NOTAMs, communications/equipment/clearances required), Terrain (obstacles, elevation, routes, minimum safe altitude MSA, minimum en route altitude MEA), Airports (runway conditions, services available, NOTAMs, runway closures)

flashcards.front: What should be done regarding: External pressures identification: Time pressure (schedul...?
flashcards.back: External pressures identification: Time pressure (schedule, deadlines, running late - pressure to fly even when conditions marginal), Financial pressure (cost of cancellation, fuel costs, rental costs - pressure to fly to avoid costs), Passenger pressure (expectations, commitments, waiting passengers - pressure to fly to meet expectations), Personal pressure (pride, ego, proving something, not wanting to cancel - pressure to fly to maintain image). Recognize and resist pressures - safety is priority, external pressures should not affect safety decisions

flashcards.front: What should be done regarding: Go/no-go decision-making: Evaluate all PAVE factors syste...?
flashcards.back: Go/no-go decision-making: Evaluate all PAVE factors systematically (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures). If all factors are acceptable (pilot ready, aircraft airworthy, environment suitable, pressures manageable), decision is GO - flight can be conducted safely. If any factor is questionable (pilot not ready, aircraft not airworthy, environment not suitable, pressures significant), decision is NO-GO - flight should not be conducted. Always have alternatives ready (delay, cancel, change route/aircraft/pilot). Continue to monitor conditions - if any factor changes, re-evaluate decision

flashcards.front: What should be done regarding: Risk management: Preflight assessment is fundamental to r...?
flashcards.back: Risk management: Preflight assessment is fundamental to risk management. Systematic evaluation of all PAVE factors enables identification of hazards and assessment of risk level. If any factor is questionable, risk is elevated - decision should be NO-GO. Alternatives provide risk mitigation - delay, cancel, change route/aircraft/pilot reduce risk. Safety is priority - always prioritize safety over external pressures

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Not evaluating all PAVE factors systematically - skipping factors (e.g., only checking weather, not checking pilot readiness or external pressures) leads to incomplete assessment and unsafe decisions

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Rationalizing questionable factors away - minimizing concerns (e.g., 'weather is marginal but improving' when visibility is 2.5 miles) leads to unsafe decisions and increased risk

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Letting external pressures affect safety decisions - allowing time, financial, passenger, or personal pressures to influence go/no-go decision when factors are questionable leads to unsafe operations

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?
flashcards.back: Not using IMSAFE checklist for pilot assessment - skipping systematic pilot evaluation (e.g., not checking fatigue, stress, medication) leads to incomplete pilot readiness assessment

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?

flashcards.front: What is a common error in Preflight Assessment?

flashcards.front: What is objective 1 for Flight Deck Management?
flashcards.back: Organize the cockpit effectively including checklists (preflight, engine start, taxi, before takeoff, cruise, descent, landing, emergency - accessible locations: knee board, checklist holder, electronic device), charts (sectional charts, airport diagrams, approach plates, NOTAMs - organized for easy access), equipment (flashlight, headset, iPad/tablet, pens, calculator, fuel tester - consistent locations, easy to reach, secure), personal items (water, snacks, sunglasses, phone - secure location, won't interfere), and emergency items (fire extinguisher, first aid kit, emergency checklist, ELT, survival equipment - known location, easy to access)

flashcards.front: What is objective 2 for Flight Deck Management?
flashcards.back: Use checklists properly including methods (read-do: read item, do action, check complete; challenge-response: challenge item, verify response, check complete), timing (preflight before engine start, engine start during start, taxi before taxi, before takeoff before takeoff, cruise during cruise, descent before descent, landing before landing, emergency when needed), and systematic usage (don't skip items, use at appropriate times, ensure nothing missed)

flashcards.front: What is objective 3 for Flight Deck Management?
flashcards.back: Prioritize tasks effectively using the aviate-navigate-communicate priority order (aviate: fly aircraft, maintain control, maintain safe flight - highest priority; navigate: know position, know route, follow route - second priority; communicate: talk to ATC, talk to passengers, handle radios - third priority), task management (prioritize tasks, defer non-essential tasks, use checklists, stay ahead of aircraft), and workload management (reduce workload, defer tasks when needed, ask for help, say unable when workload too high)

flashcards.front: What is objective 1 for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Perform pre-start checks including area clear (check propeller area clear of people, equipment, obstacles - announce 'Clear!' before starting), controls set (flight controls free and correct, trim set for takeoff, parking brake set if available, throttle idle position, mixture idle cutoff or as required, propeller high RPM if controllable), fuel system checked (fuel selector on proper tank, fuel quantity adequate, fuel pump on if required, mixture idle cutoff for carbureted or full rich for fuel-injected), and electrical system checked (master switch off before start, avionics off before start, lights as required, battery adequate charge)

flashcards.front: What is objective 2 for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Start the engine correctly following POH procedures including starting sequence (master switch on, fuel pump on if required, mixture idle cutoff for carbureted or full rich for fuel-injected, throttle cracked 1/4 to 1/2 inch, starter engage, monitor engine, mixture rich when engine fires for carbureted), carbureted engine procedures (mixture idle cutoff before start, throttle cracked, starter engage, when engine fires move mixture to rich immediately, monitor engine, adjust throttle), fuel-injected engine procedures (mixture full rich before start, throttle cracked, fuel pump on if required, starter engage, monitor engine, adjust throttle), and monitoring (watch oil pressure should rise, RPM should stabilize, engine instruments normal indications, engine sound smooth running)

flashcards.front: What is objective 3 for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Handle hot starts correctly including recognizing hot engine conditions (engine hot from recent operation, fuel vaporizes, difficult to start), hot start procedure (mixture idle cutoff for carbureted, throttle full open, crank engine to clear fuel, mixture rich, throttle cracked, starter engage), and troubleshooting (if engine doesn't start, stop starter, troubleshoot, try again with reduced fuel)

flashcards.front: What is objective 4 for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Respond to engine fires immediately including recognizing engine fire (fire visible, smoke, fuel smell), fire procedures (continue cranking first to draw fuel into engine and may extinguish fire, mixture idle cutoff to stop fuel, throttle full open to clear fuel, master switch off to stop electrical and fuel pump, evacuate if fire persists), and fire prevention (don't over-prime, check for fuel leaks, use proper starting procedure, monitor during start)

flashcards.front: What is objective 5 for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Perform post-start checks including oil pressure (must rise within 30 seconds, critical indicator, if no pressure shut down immediately), RPM (should stabilize at idle, smooth operation, if rough or unstable troubleshoot or shut down), engine instruments (oil pressure normal, oil temperature warming up, fuel pressure normal, RPM stable, ammeter charging - all should show normal indications), systems (electrical charging and voltage normal, fuel flow normal and no leaks, controls free and correct, avionics can turn on after warm-up), and taxi readiness (engine running smoothly, oil pressure normal, systems operational, controls free, clear to taxi)

flashcards.front: What is objective 6 for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Teach engine starting to students effectively explaining pre-start checks, starting procedures (carbureted and fuel-injected), hot start procedures, engine fire procedures, and post-start checks with integrated scenarios with specific numbers and conditions

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Always announce 'Clear!' loudly before engaging the starter — ensure the propeller area is free of people and obstacles

flashcards.front: What should be done regarding: Oil pressure must rise within 30 seconds of engine start;...?
flashcards.back: Oil pressure must rise within 30 seconds of engine start; if it does not, shut down immediately to prevent engine damage

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: For carbureted engines: mixture idle cutoff before start, then move to rich when engine fires; for fuel-injected: mixture full rich before start

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Hot start procedure differs significantly from cold start — recognize when engine is heat-soaked and adjust technique accordingly

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Engine fire during start: continue cranking to draw fuel into engine, mixture idle cutoff, throttle full open, master off, evacuate if fire persists

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Never over-prime the engine — excess fuel is the primary cause of engine fires during start

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Post-start verification sequence: oil pressure, RPM stable, engine instruments green, electrical system charging, controls free

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Teach students to develop a flow pattern for pre-start checks rather than relying solely on a checklist

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Engine Starting?
flashcards.back: Each aircraft type has specific starting procedures in the POH — never assume procedures transfer between aircraft

flashcards.back: Always use Manufacturer Checklists

flashcards.back: Anti-collision lights should be turned on prior to any start, at night use position lights too

flashcards.back: Always call “CLEAR” out of the side window and wait for a response

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Power application - apply full power smoothly but decisively, smooth application prevents excessive yaw, decisive application ensures climb performance

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Rudder control - apply right rudder immediately with power, power causes left yaw that must be counteracted, insufficient rudder causes left turn and loss of control

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Pitch control - pitch for VY immediately after power, pitching up before power causes settling, VY provides best climb performance and prevents settling

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Flap retraction - retract flaps incrementally, not all at once, retracting all flaps causes significant sink, follow POH procedure for flap retraction sequence

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Settling prevention - power must be applied before pitch, pitching up without power causes airplane to settle, settling can result in ground contact or obstacle strike

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Radio communication - announce 'Going around' on radio immediately, other traffic needs to know, communication prevents conflicts in pattern

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Decision criteria - recognize unstabilized approach early, too high/low, too fast/slow, not aligned, obstacles, or traffic require go-around, don't try to salvage bad approaches

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Pattern re-entry - climb to pattern altitude after go-around, re-enter pattern properly, don't cut off other traffic, follow standard pattern procedures

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Student hesitation - be ready to take controls if student hesitates, delayed go-around is dangerous, encourage immediate decision and execution

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Multiple go-arounds - multiple go-arounds are acceptable, don't pressure student to land, safety always trumps completion, professional pilots do multiple go-arounds

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?
flashcards.back: Crosswind considerations - go-around in crosswind requires additional rudder, maintain runway alignment during climb, be ready for wind effects during climb

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Go-Around / Rejected Landing?

flashcards.back: Whenever safety dictates

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes?
flashcards.back: Spatial disorientation - unusual attitudes can cause severe disorientation, must recognize unusual attitude immediately, apply proper recovery technique, be ready to take controls if student becomes disoriented, have safety pilot if possible

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes?
flashcards.back: Altitude loss - unusual attitudes can cause rapid altitude loss, must maintain adequate altitude (minimum 4000 AGL), monitor altitude constantly, be ready to take controls if altitude loss is excessive

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes?
flashcards.back: Stall risk - nose-high unusual attitude can lead to stall, must reduce angle of attack immediately, level wings, be ready to take controls if student delays recovery

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes?
flashcards.back: Excessive airspeed risk - nose-low unusual attitude can lead to excessive airspeed, must reduce angle of attack immediately but don't overcorrect, monitor airspeed indicator, be ready to take controls if airspeed becomes excessive

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes?
flashcards.back: Spin risk - unusual attitude with bank can lead to spin entry, must level wings immediately, maintain coordination, be ready to recover from spin if it occurs

flashcards.front: What is an important safety consideration for Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes?
flashcards.back: Traffic awareness - instrument flight requires increased traffic awareness, students focused on recovery may miss traffic, emphasize see-and-avoid when possible, use safety pilot if available

flashcards.front: Why is this a problem: Procedure: Reduce power to idle (maximizes descent rate),...?

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Engine Failure During Takeoff Before VMC (Simulated)?
flashcards.back: Procedure: Recognize engine failure (engine quits, loss of power on one side, asymmetric thrust, yaw toward inoperative engine), Maintain directional control (apply full rudder opposite to inoperative engine, maintain runway centerline, avoid overcorrection), Abort takeoff (reduce power on operating engine to idle, apply brakes, maintain directional control, bring aircraft to safe stop), Secure inoperative engine (mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector off, magnetos off, close cowl flaps)
flashcards.lessonTitle: Engine Failure During Takeoff Before VMC (Simulated)

flashcards.front: What should be done regarding: Directional control: Apply full rudder opposite to inoper...?
flashcards.back: Directional control: Apply full rudder opposite to inoperative engine, maintain runway centerline - below VMC, directional control cannot be maintained, must abort takeoff
flashcards.lessonTitle: Engine Failure During Takeoff Before VMC (Simulated)

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Engine Failure During Takeoff Before VMC (Simulated)?
flashcards.back: Abort procedure: Reduce power on operating engine to idle (reduces asymmetric thrust, makes directional control easier), Apply brakes (firmly but smoothly, don't lock brakes, maintain directional control), Maintain directional control (maintain runway centerline, avoid overcorrection), Bring aircraft to safe stop (stop on runway if possible, clear runway if needed, secure aircraft)
flashcards.lessonTitle: Engine Failure During Takeoff Before VMC (Simulated)

flashcards.back: Airspeed effects: High airspeed (90-100 knots or higher) - better directional control (more rudder effectiveness, easier to maintain heading, less yaw), Low airspeed (approaching VMC) - less directional control (less rudder effectiveness, harder to maintain heading, more yaw, approaching VMC)
flashcards.lessonTitle: Demonstration of Effects of Various Airspeeds and Configurations during Engine Inoperative

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Demonstration of Effects of Various Airspeeds and Configurations during Engine Inoperative?
flashcards.back: Configuration effects: Clean configuration - better performance (less drag, better climb performance, better speed), higher VMC (clean configuration typically has higher VMC, more margin above VMC), easier to maintain control (less drag, less yaw, easier directional control), Gear down - increased drag (gear down increases drag, reduces performance), lower VMC (gear down typically lowers VMC, less margin above VMC), more rudder required (increased drag increases yaw, requires more rudder), Flaps down - increased drag (flaps down increases drag, reduces performance), lower VMC (flaps down typically lowers VMC, less margin above VMC), more rudder required (increased drag increases yaw, requires more rudder)
flashcards.lessonTitle: Demonstration of Effects of Various Airspeeds and Configurations during Engine Inoperative

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Demonstration of Effects of Various Airspeeds and Configurations during Engine Inoperative?
flashcards.back: Procedure: Establish one engine inoperative (simulate one engine inoperative, maintain directional control, maintain airspeed above VMC), Demonstrate various airspeeds (high airspeed 90-100 knots, medium airspeed 75-85 knots, low airspeed approaching VMC, observe effects on directional control and handling), Demonstrate various configurations (clean configuration, gear down, flaps down, observe effects on directional control, performance, and VMC), Explain relationship between airspeed, configuration, and performance (higher airspeed provides better directional control, clean configuration provides better performance, gear and flaps down increase drag and lower VMC)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for Demonstration of Effects of Various Airspeeds and Configurations during Engine Inoperative?

flashcards.front: What is a key point for After Landing, Parking, and Securing?
flashcards.back: After landing, parking, and securing requires following proper procedures systematically

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for After Landing, Parking, and Securing?
flashcards.back: After landing procedures: Clear runway promptly (exit runway promptly, clear runway completely, follow taxi instructions, maintain situational awareness), Taxi to parking (follow taxi instructions, maintain safe taxi speed typically 10-15 knots, maintain situational awareness, watch for other aircraft and vehicles), Follow airport procedures (follow airport signs and markings, follow ATC instructions if applicable, maintain communication if required)

flashcards.front: Why is this a problem: Parking procedures: Position aircraft properly (position ...?
flashcards.back: Parking procedures: Position aircraft properly (position aircraft in designated parking area, ensure adequate clearance from other aircraft typically 10-15 feet minimum, position for easy access and egress, consider wind direction), Set parking brake (set parking brake firmly, verify parking brake is set, ensure aircraft will not move), Chock wheels (place chocks in front of and behind wheels, ensure chocks are properly positioned, verify aircraft is secure)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for After Landing, Parking, and Securing?
flashcards.back: Securing procedures: Shut down engine properly (reduce power to idle, mixture idle cutoff, turn off magnetos, turn off master switch, verify engine is shut down), Secure controls (set controls to neutral position, secure control locks if applicable, verify controls are secure), Secure systems (turn off all electrical equipment, turn off fuel pump if applicable, secure fuel selector, verify all systems are secure)

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for After Landing, Parking, and Securing?
flashcards.back: Postflight inspection: Inspect aircraft exterior (inspect for damage, inspect for leaks, inspect for loose items, note any discrepancies), Inspect aircraft interior (inspect for damage, inspect for loose items, verify all equipment is secure, note any discrepancies), Document discrepancies (note discrepancies in logbook if required, report discrepancies to maintenance if required, ensure discrepancies are addressed)

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for After Landing, Parking, and Securing?
flashcards.back: Documentation: Complete logbook entries (enter flight time, enter flight date, enter aircraft identification, enter pilot information, note any discrepancies), Complete flight records (complete flight log if required, complete maintenance log if required, complete any other required records), File flight plan closure (close flight plan if opened, notify FSS if required, ensure flight plan is properly closed)

flashcards.front: What is a key point for After Landing, Parking, and Securing?
flashcards.back: Follow the procedures outlined on the manufacturer’s checklist

flashcards.back: Post-landing procedures: Taxi on water after landing (maintain control, maintain safe speed typically 5-10 knots, maintain situational awareness, watch for obstacles and other watercraft), Approach dock/beach (approach dock or beach area, maintain control, maintain safe speed, maintain situational awareness, consider wind and current), Select appropriate securing method (choose anchoring, docking, mooring, or beaching based on conditions and availability, consider wind, current, and water depth)

flashcards.back: Anchoring procedures: Select anchor location (select suitable anchor location, consider water depth typically 10-20 feet, consider bottom type, consider wind and current, ensure adequate clearance), Deploy anchor (approach anchor location, reduce speed, deploy anchor from bow, allow anchor to set, verify anchor is holding), Secure anchor (secure anchor line to aircraft, verify anchor line is secure, verify anchor is holding, ensure adequate scope typically 5:1 to 7:1 ratio), Secure aircraft (shut down engine, secure controls, secure systems)

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Seaplane Post-Landing Procedures?
flashcards.back: Docking procedures: Approach dock (approach dock into wind or current, maintain control, maintain safe speed typically 2-5 knots, maintain situational awareness), Secure to dock (approach dock slowly, use dock lines to secure aircraft, secure bow line first, secure stern line, verify all lines are secure), Secure aircraft (shut down engine, secure controls, secure systems)

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Seaplane Post-Landing Procedures?
flashcards.back: Mooring procedures: Approach mooring (approach mooring buoy or float, maintain control, maintain safe speed typically 2-5 knots), Secure to mooring (approach mooring slowly, attach mooring line to aircraft, secure bow line to mooring, verify all lines are secure), Secure aircraft (shut down engine, secure controls, secure systems)

flashcards.front: What must be maintained for Seaplane Post-Landing Procedures?
flashcards.back: Ramping/Beaching procedures: Approach beach/ramp (approach beach or ramp area, maintain control, maintain safe speed typically 2-5 knots), Beach aircraft (approach beach/ramp slowly, ground aircraft on beach/ramp, ensure aircraft is properly positioned), Secure aircraft (shut down engine, secure controls, secure systems, consider tide if applicable)
